mainTopic: שבועת העדות: when witnesses are exempt, and which oath wordings and names of God make them liable
overview: This amud opens by finishing an earlier point: since שבועת העדות leaves out the word "ונעלם," even a witness who swears falsely on purpose (מזיד) brings a קרבן. Then a משנה lists five cases where witnesses who falsely deny knowing testimony are exempt. They are exempt when the testimony is not about a real money claim, when the oath came before they knew anything, when the oath was called out to a general crowd, when they are unfit to testify, and when the demand did not come from the תובע himself. The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a פסוק as the source for each case, and רבי אלעזר reads "אם לוא יגיד" as "to him," meaning the plaintiff. A second משנה teaches which wordings count as an oath, and that God's names and descriptions count while heaven and earth do not. It also covers cursing with these names, where רבי מאיר and the חכמים disagree. In the גמרא, רב יהודה and then אביי explain how "משביעני עליכם" works without God's name. The amud ends with a contradiction: a ברייתא says חנון ורחום may be erased. אביי begins to answer that the משנה means "by the One Who is gracious."

steps.title: Why the Torah places the oath of testimony next to sections that say 'it was hidden'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the Torah puts שבועת העדות right next to שבועת ביטוי and טומאת מקדש וקדשיו to show a contrast. Those sections say "ונעלם" and this one does not, which teaches that a מזיד is liable just like a שוגג.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why the Torah wrote the oath of testimony next to the oath on an utterance and next to becoming impure in the מקדש or with holy foods. In all of those, the Torah says "and it was hidden," but here it does not. This teaches that someone who swears falsely on purpose is liable, just like someone who did it by mistake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes answering a question from just before this section. It explains why the Torah placed these sections next to each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sections around שבועת העדות in the פסוקים say "ונעלם," meaning the person forgot or did not realize. Those sections only bring a קרבן for a mistake. Since שבועת העדות sits right beside them and leaves that word out, the Torah is pointing out a difference: here even a deliberate false oath brings a קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, a name for ה׳ as the One who gave the Torah
An oath on an utterance, swearing to do or not do something
Entering the מקדש or eating holy food while impure
"And it was hidden", meaning the person forgot or did not realize
Someone who acts on purpose
Someone who acts by mistake

steps.whatToRemember: For שבועת העדות, a witness who falsely swears he knows nothing brings a קרבן even if he did it on purpose. That is unlike the other sections nearby, which say "ונעלם."
steps.confusionAlert: Usually a קרבן is only for a שוגג. שבועת העדות is an unusual exception where a מזיד also brings a קרבן, and that is exactly what this line is teaching.

phrases.english: For this reason the Merciful One wrote [the oath of] testimony
next to the oath on an utterance
and next to the impurity of the Temple and its holy foods
for in all of them it says "and it was hidden,"
but here it does not say "and it was hidden";
to make one liable for the intentional like the unintentional.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a question raised before this section about why these sections are placed together
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains placement in the Torah as a deliberate contrast
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The placement of these sections next to each other might have seemed to have no purpose
steps.terutzMaskana: The placement highlights the missing word "ונעלם", teaching that a מזיד is liable in שבועת העדות

steps.title: No liability when the testimony is about a promised gift
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if the testimony would only prove that someone promised a gift, the witnesses are exempt. Liability applies only to a monetary claim like a פקדון.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says to witnesses: "I make you swear: if you do not come and testify for me that so-and-so said he would give me 200 זוז and did not give it," they are exempt. One is liable only for a claim of money, like a deposit.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. Its first case shows that the oath of testimony only counts when the testimony would actually make someone pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A deposit is real money that is owed, so testimony about it would force payment. A mere statement that someone would give a gift does not create a debt that the court collects. So refusing that testimony is not the kind of oath the Torah punishes.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
"I put you under oath", the formula for making witnesses swear
Exempt, meaning they do not bring the קרבן
A claim for money
A deposit left with someone for safekeeping

phrases.english: MISHNA: "I put you under oath,
if you do not come and testify for me
that so-and-so said

phrases.aramaic: לִיתֵּן לִי מָאתַיִם זוּז וְלֹא נָתַן״ –
phrases.english: he would give me two hundred זוז, and he did not give"
these are exempt,
for one is liable only
for a claim of money, like a deposit.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַשְׁבִּיעַ אֲנִי עֲלֵיכֶם, אִם לֹא תָבוֹאוּ וּתְעִידוּנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath of testimony applies only when the testimony would establish an actual monetary claim, like a פקדון

steps.title: No liability when the oath came before the witnesses knew anything
steps.stepSummary: If he makes them swear ahead of time to testify whenever they learn something, they are exempt, because the oath came before the testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says: "I make you swear that when you know testimony for me, you will come and testify," they are exempt, because the oath came before the testimony.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the משנה's second case of exemption. Here the problem is the timing of the oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the moment of the oath, the witnesses did not yet know anything. So it was not a refusal to give testimony they had. The oath of testimony only counts when the witnesses already know the facts at the time they are asked to swear.

keyTerms.meaning: The oath came before the testimony, meaning before they knew the facts
"When you will know", referring to the future

phrases.english: "I put you under oath
that when you will know testimony for me
you will come and testify for me"
these are exempt,
because the oath came before the testimony.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַשְׁבִּיעַ אֲנִי עֲלֵיכֶם כְּשֶׁתֵּדְעוּ לִי עֵדוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second exemption case in the same משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath given before the witnesses know the testimony does not make them liable

steps.title: No liability when the oath is called out to a general crowd
steps.stepSummary: If he stands in the בית הכנסת and calls out the oath to everyone, the people are exempt until he aims it at specific people.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he stood in the בית הכנסת and said: "I make you swear that if you know testimony for me, you will come and testify," they are exempt until he directs it at them specifically.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the משנה's third case of exemption. The problem here is that the oath was not aimed at anyone in particular.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the people may already know the facts, so the timing is fine. But a general call to a crowd is not a real demand placed on specific witnesses. Liability starts only when he intends to address particular people.

keyTerms.meaning: Synagogue
He intends it for them, meaning he aims the oath at specific people

steps.whatToRemember: So far the משנה has given three ways witnesses are exempt: the testimony is not a real money claim, the oath came before they knew anything, or the oath was not aimed at specific people. The next two steps add two more cases: witnesses unfit to testify, and a demand that did not come from the תובע himself.

phrases.english: If he stood in the synagogue and said:
"I put you under oath,
that if you know testimony for me
you will come and testify for me"
these are exempt,
until he directs it at them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third exemption case in the same משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general oath called out to a crowd does not make anyone liable unless it is aimed at specific witnesses

steps.title: Unfit witnesses are exempt
steps.stepSummary: If the witnesses' knowledge is only hearsay, or one of them is a relative or disqualified, they are exempt even though they swore falsely.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said to two people: 'I make you swear, so-and-so and so-and-so, that if you know testimony for me, you will come and testify for me.' They answered: 'We swear we do not know any testimony for you.' In fact they did know something, but only secondhand from another witness. Or one of them was a relative or disqualified. These witnesses are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives another case where witnesses who falsely deny knowing testimony are not liable: their testimony could never have counted in בית דין anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שבועת העדות only makes witnesses liable when their testimony could actually have helped the plaintiff. Hearsay (עד מפי עד) is not accepted. A קרוב or פסול witness cannot testify. So here the false oath did not take away anything the plaintiff could have used.

keyTerms.meaning: A witness repeating what he heard from another witness (hearsay), which is not valid testimony
A relative, who is disqualified from testifying
Disqualified from serving as a witness
Exempt from liability

phrases.english: He said to two people:
"I make you swear, so-and-so and so-and-so,
that if you know testimony for me
you will come and testify for me,"
[and they said:] "We swear we do not know testimony for you";
phrases.notes: The words 'and they said' are not written. The גמרא assumes you know this is the witnesses answering.

phrases.english: and they do know testimony for him,
but only a witness from the mouth of a witness,
phrases.notes: Meaning they didn't see it themselves. They only heard about it from someone who did.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁהָיָה אֶחָד מֵהֶן קָרוֹב אוֹ פָּסוּל –
phrases.english: or one of them was a relative or disqualified –
these are exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לִשְׁנַיִם: מַשְׁבִּיעַ אֲנִי עֲלֵיכֶם אִישׁ פְּלוֹנִי וּפְלוֹנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of exemptions, now about witnesses whose testimony would not be valid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses whose testimony would be invalid (hearsay, a relative, or a פסול witness) are exempt from שבועת העדות.

steps.title: The demand must come from the plaintiff himself
steps.stepSummary: If the plaintiff sent his slave to make the demand, or the defendant made the witnesses swear, they are exempt until they hear the demand from the plaintiff himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the plaintiff sent the demand through his slave, or the defendant said to the witnesses, 'I make you swear that if you know testimony for him, you will come and testify for him,' the witnesses are exempt. They become liable only once they hear the demand from the plaintiff himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds that the oath must come directly from the person who would gain from the testimony, the תובע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A message passed through his עבד is not enough. An oath from the נתבע, who is the other side, is also not enough. Liability only starts when the witnesses hear the demand straight from the mouth of the תובע.

keyTerms.meaning: His slave
The defendant, the one being sued
The plaintiff, the one making the claim

steps.whatToRemember: For שבועת העדות to make witnesses liable, the testimony must be valid, and the oath must come directly from the תובע.

phrases.english: If he sent it through his slave,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the plaintiff. He sent his slave to make the witnesses swear instead of doing it himself.

phrases.english: or the defendant said to them:
"I make you swear
that if you know testimony for him
you will come and testify for him" –
these are exempt,
until they hear it from the mouth of the plaintiff.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another exemption in the משנה. Like Step 4, it is about who must make the demand and to whom.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses are liable only if the plaintiff himself makes them swear, not his slave and not the defendant.

steps.title: Source that a promised gift is excluded
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא raises the case of testimony about a promised gift of two hundred זוז. One might think the witnesses are liable, but the word ״תחטא״ sets up a גזירה שוה that excludes it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'I make you swear: if you do not come and testify for me that so-and-so said he would give me two hundred זוז and did not give them...' One might think the witnesses would be liable. So the פסוק says ״תחטא״ here and ״תחטא״ there, to make a גזירה שוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא that gives the Torah source for the משנה's rule from Step 2, that testimony about a promised gift does not create liability. This step only names the tool, a גזירה שוה; the next step spells it out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ״יכול״ shows why a source is needed: you might think any demand to testify counts. The answer is a גזירה שוה, which links two passages that use the same word, ״תחטא״, so a rule from one carries over to the other.

keyTerms.meaning: One might have thought: sets up a wrong assumption the source will rule out
The verse teaches: introduces the Torah source
A link between two passages that use the same word, so a law in one applies to the other
'Shall sin': the shared word in both passages

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
"I make you swear
if you do not come and testify for me

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאָמַר אִישׁ פְּלוֹנִי לִיתֵּן לִי מָאתַיִם זוּז
phrases.english: that so-and-so said he would give me two hundred zuz
and he did not give" –
one might think they would be liable?
The verse teaches:
"shall sin" – "shall sin" for a verbal comparison.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַשְׁבִּיעַנִי עֲלֵיכֶם אִם לֹא תָבוֹאוּ וּתְעִידוּנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the משנה and starts the גמרא by giving the Torah source for the gift rule from Step 2.
steps.raayaObject: The משנה's rule that testimony about a promised gift does not create liability for שבועת העדות
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא using a גזירה שוה on ״תחטא״ in ויקרא 5:1 and ויקרא 5:21

steps.title: Spelling out the comparison: a real money claim
steps.stepSummary: The oath about a פקדון deals with a money claim the plaintiff truly has. So שבועת העדות too applies only to a real money claim that is truly owed.
steps.simpleTranslation: It says ״תחטא״ here, and it says ״תחטא״ there. Just as there it is about a money claim that he really has, so here too it is about a money claim that he really has.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now spells out the גזירה שוה and finishes the proof from the previous step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The passage about denying a פקדון is clearly about money the claimant is really owed. Because of the shared word, שבועת העדות gets the same limit. A promised gift is not owed (״יש לו״ is missing), so the witnesses are exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: A monetary claim
And he has it: the claimant is truly owed the money
Here / there: the two passages being compared

steps.whatToRemember: שבועת העדות requires testimony about a real money claim that is truly owed. A promise to give a gift does not qualify, as we learn from the גזירה שוה of ״תחטא״ with the oath about a פקדון.
steps.confusionAlert: ״יש לו״ is not about whether the defendant can pay. It means the plaintiff has a real legal claim. A mere promise of a gift is not owed, so it fails this test.
steps.whyThisMatters: This one comparison explains why testimony that would only prove a gift promise cannot create liability: the Torah ties this oath to real money claims.

phrases.english: It says here "shall sin,"
and it says there "shall sin";
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:21, the passage about falsely denying a פקדון.

phrases.aramaic: מָה לְהַלָּן בִּתְבִיעַת מָמוֹן – וְיֵשׁ לוֹ,
phrases.english: just as there it is about a money claim – and he has it,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּאן בִּתְבִיעַת מָמוֹן – וְיֵשׁ לוֹ.
phrases.english: so too here it is about a money claim – and he has it.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶאֱמַר כָּאן תֶּחֱטָא, וְנֶאֱמַר לְהַלָּן תֶּחֱטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the גזירה שוה named in Step 7 and finishes the proof.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Like the oath about a פקדון, שבועת העדות applies only to a real money claim that is truly owed, so testimony about a promised gift does not create liability.

steps.title: The oath must come after the witnesses already know the testimony
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of an oath about testimony the witnesses will know in the future. A ברייתא uses a פסוק to show they are exempt, because the knowledge must come before the oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'I make you swear that when you know testimony for me...' The רבנן taught: if someone says, 'I make you swear that when you know testimony for me you will come and testify for me,' you might think they are liable. So the פסוק says, 'and he heard the voice of an oath, and he is a witness, or he saw or he knew.' This means someone whose knowledge of the testimony came before the oath. It does not mean someone whose oath came before the testimony.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה and brings a ברייתא with a פסוק that explains why these witnesses are exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the oath is given before the witnesses know anything. The פסוק says 'he heard the oath, and he is a witness,' which means he was already a witness when he heard it. So an oath about testimony they will learn later does not create liability.

keyTerms.meaning: 'One might think': it sets up a mistaken idea that the פסוק will then reject
'The פסוק teaches': it brings the verse that settles the question
'The voice of an oath': the oath the plaintiff puts on the witnesses
'Came first' or 'preceded'

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the witnesses are exempt because they lied about nothing. The point is about order: knowing the testimony has to come first, and the oath second.

phrases.english: "I administer an oath upon you
that when you will know testimony for me," etc.
The Rabbis taught:
"I administer an oath upon you
that when you will know testimony for me
you will come and testify for me"
one might think they would be liable?
The verse teaches: "And he heard the voice of an oath

phrases.aramaic: וְהוּא עֵד אוֹ רָאָה אוֹ יָדַע״ –
phrases.english: and he is a witness, or he saw or he knew"
one whose testimony came before the oath,
and not one whose oath came before the testimony.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next case in the משנה and gives the פסוק behind it.
steps.raayaObject: The משנה's ruling that an oath about future testimony does not make the witnesses liable.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading ויקרא 5:1, 'and he is a witness', to mean the person was already a witness when the oath was given.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets a basic rule of שבועת העדות: the oath only works on witnesses who already have the testimony.

steps.title: A general oath in the בית הכנסת, even with his witnesses present
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of calling out the oath in the בית הכנסת, and שמואל adds that the people are exempt even if his real witnesses are in the crowd.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he stood in the בית הכנסת and said, 'I make you swear.' שמואל said: they are exempt even if his witnesses are among them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה about an oath called out to everyone in the בית הכנסת, and שמואל adds a detail to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already said that a general oath to a crowd does not bind anyone. שמואל adds that this is true even when the actual witnesses are in that crowd, because the oath was not aimed at them.

keyTerms.meaning: Synagogue, a public place full of people
'His witnesses are among them': the people who really know the testimony are in the crowd

phrases.english: If he stood in the synagogue
and said, "I administer an oath upon you."
שמואל said:
Even if his witnesses are among them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line of the משנה, the one summarized in step 4, and adds שמואל's comment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general oath called out in the בית הכנסת does not bind the witnesses, even if they are present in the crowd.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why שמואל needs to say this. If his witnesses weren't there, the משנה's ruling would teach nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's statement as something we already knew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's case only makes sense if the witnesses were in the crowd. Otherwise there would be no one to exempt. So what is שמואל adding?

keyTerms.meaning: 'It's obvious!': a challenge saying a statement teaches nothing new

phrases.english: That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's addition in step 10 as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's statement 'even if his witnesses are among them'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's case only matters if the witnesses are present, so שמואל seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The new point: even when he stands right next to them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that שמואל means a case where he stands right beside the witnesses. We might have treated that like speaking to them directly, so שמואל teaches that they are still exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where he is standing right next to them. You might have said it is as if he spoke to them directly, so it teaches us that it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing שמואל's case to one where the plaintiff stands right next to the witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Standing next to the witnesses might look like aiming the oath at them. שמואל teaches that the oath still binds no one, because he did not say it to them specifically.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is only needed for...': it narrows a ruling to a specific case where it teaches something new
'Standing over them': standing right beside them
'You might have said': it brings up the mistaken idea being ruled out
'It teaches us': the new point being taught

steps.whatToRemember: An oath called out to a crowd binds no one, even witnesses standing right next to the speaker. The oath has to be aimed at specific people.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where he stands right next to them;

phrases.aramaic: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר לְהוּ דָּמֵי,
phrases.english: you might have said it is as if he spoke to them directly,
so it teaches us that it is not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Standing right next to the witnesses could count as speaking to them directly, which would make them liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even then they are exempt, because the oath was not aimed at them specifically.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Only an oath aimed at specific people binds the witnesses. Being nearby is not enough.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports שמואל about witnesses inside a crowd
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if someone puts a whole crowd under oath and his witnesses are among them, they are exempt because he did not single them out. If he says 'everyone standing here,' they are liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also taught this way: Someone saw a group of people standing, and his witnesses were among them. He said to them, 'I make you swear that if you know testimony for me, you will come and testify for me.' You might think they are liable. The פסוק says 'and he is a witness,' and here he did not single out his witnesses. You might think the same is true even if he said 'everyone standing here.' The פסוק says 'and he is a witness,' and here he did single out his witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up what שמואל said: witnesses who are mixed into a crowd are exempt when the plaintiff speaks to the crowd in general.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא teaches that the oath has to be aimed at the witnesses themselves. A general speech to a group does not count, even when the real witnesses are standing in it. But the words 'everyone standing here' include each person on purpose, so this counts as singling them out, and they are liable.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא (a support)
A group or crowd
He singled out his witnesses
The פסוק teaches
You might have thought

steps.confusionAlert: Speaking to a crowd is not always a problem. A general address to a group makes the witnesses exempt. Saying 'everyone standing here' makes them liable, because it purposely includes each person.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the rule for when an oath said to a group still counts as aimed at the witnesses.

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:

phrases.aramaic: רָאָה סִיעָה שֶׁל בְּנֵי אָדָם עוֹמְדִין,
phrases.english: He saw a group of people standing,
and his witnesses were among them,
and he said to them:
"I make you swear
that if you know testimony for me
you will come and testify for me" —
you might think they are liable?
The verse says: "And he is a witness" —
and here he did not single out his witnesses.
You might think the same even if he said
"everyone who is standing here"?
The verse says: "And he is a witness" —
and here he did single out his witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports שמואל's statement from step 10 that witnesses in a crowd are exempt when the oath is not aimed at them.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's rule that witnesses inside a crowd are exempt when the plaintiff speaks to the crowd in general
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that reads the words 'והוא עד'

steps.title: Witnesses who are not fit to testify are exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of an oath said to two people, then brings a ברייתא. If their testimony is only hearsay, or one of them is a relative or otherwise not allowed to testify, they are exempt, because the פסוק speaks about people who are fit to testify.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'He said to two people, I make you swear.' The רבנן taught: He said to two people, 'I make you swear, so-and-so and so-and-so, that if you know testimony for me, you will come and testify for me.' But their testimony was only hearsay, or one of them was a relative or not allowed to testify. You might think they are liable. The פסוק says 'if he does not tell, he will carry his sin.' The פסוק is speaking about people who are fit to tell.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next case in the משנה and brings a ברייתא that gives its source from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even when the plaintiff names the witnesses clearly, they are only liable if their testimony could actually be used in בית דין. 'If he does not tell' assumes that telling would mean something. Hearsay, or a witness who is a relative or otherwise not allowed to testify, could not be used, so there is no liability.

keyTerms.meaning: Hearsay: a witness repeating what another witness told him
A relative, who may not testify
Not allowed to testify
Fit to give testimony

phrases.english: He said to two people: "I make you swear."
The Sages taught: If he said to two people:
"I make you swear, so-and-so and so-and-so,
that if you know testimony for me
you will come and testify for me";

phrases.aramaic: וְהֵן יוֹדְעִין לוֹ עֵדוּת עֵד מִפִּי עֵד,
phrases.english: and they know testimony for him only as hearsay,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁהָיָה אֶחָד מֵהֶן קָרוֹב אוֹ פָּסוּל –
phrases.english: or one of them was a relative or not allowed to testify —
you might think they are liable?

phrases.aramaic: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״אִם לוֹא יַגִּיד וְנָשָׂא עֲוֹנוֹ״ –
phrases.english: The verse says: "If he does not tell, he will carry his sin" —
the verse is speaking about those who are fit to testify.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לִשְׁנַיִם: ״מַשְׁבִּיעַ אֲנִי עֲלֵיכֶם״. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next case of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses whose testimony could not be accepted (hearsay, a relative, or someone not allowed to testify) are exempt from שבועת העדות.

steps.title: An oath sent through a slave, or said by the defendant
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of sending through a slave. A ברייתא rules that both this case and the case where the defendant makes the witnesses swear are exempt, based on the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'He sent it through his slave,' and so on. The רבנן taught: He sent it through his slave, or the defendant said to them, 'I make you swear that if you know testimony for him, you will come and testify for him.' You might think they are liable. The פסוק says 'if he does not tell, he will carry his sin.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next case in the משנה and brings a ברייתא that exempts the witnesses, using the same פסוק. It does not explain the proof yet. That comes in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two cases here. In the first, the plaintiff does not ask the witnesses himself but sends his slave. In the second, the person making them swear is the defendant, not the plaintiff. The ברייתא exempts both, and steps 16 and 17 explain how the פסוק proves this.

keyTerms.meaning: He sent it through his slave
The defendant, the one being sued

phrases.english: He sent it through his slave, etc.
The Sages taught: If he sent it through his slave,
or the defendant said to them:

phrases.aramaic: ״מַשְׁבִּיעַנִי עֲלֵיכֶם שֶׁאִם אַתֶּם יוֹדְעִין לוֹ עֵדוּת
phrases.english: "I make you swear that if you know testimony for him
you will come and testify for him" —
phrases.notes: 'Him' means the plaintiff. The defendant is asking them to testify for the other side.

phrases.english: you might think they are liable?

phrases.aramaic: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״אִם לֹא יַגִּיד וְנָשָׂא עֲוֹנוֹ״.
phrases.english: The verse says: "If he does not tell, he will carry his sin."

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁלַּח בְּיַד עַבְדּוֹ וְכוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next case of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath sent through the plaintiff's slave, or said by the defendant, does not make the witnesses liable.

steps.title: How does the פסוק teach this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the words 'אם לא יגיד' show that these cases are exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the proof from the פסוק?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the פסוק proves the ruling of the ברייתא, which is not clear from a simple reading. This sets up רבי אלעזר's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same פסוק was used in step 14 to teach that the witnesses must be fit to testify. Here it is used for something different: who has to ask them. The גמרא wants to know which part of the פסוק teaches that.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the proof from the פסוק?

phrases.english: What is the derivation?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the פסוק quoted in step 15 proves its ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which detail of 'אם לא יגיד' shows that a slave's message or the defendant's oath does not create liability

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: 'לוא' is read as 'to him'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains that the word is spelled לוא, so it can also be read as לו, 'to him.' The witness is liable only if he refuses to tell the plaintiff himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: It is written 'אם לוא יגיד.' Read it as: if he does not tell 'to him,' he will carry his sin. But if he does not tell someone else, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the question: the unusual spelling of one word in the פסוק teaches that only the plaintiff's own demand counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual spelling of 'not' is לא, but here it is written לוא, which holds the word לו, 'to him.' So the פסוק means: if he does not tell him, meaning the plaintiff who asked. When the request comes from a slave or from the defendant, the person asking is 'someone else,' so the witnesses are exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written (how the word is spelled in the פסוק)
To him
To someone else
Exempt

steps.whatToRemember: Witnesses are liable for שבועת העדות only if the plaintiff himself singles them out, they are fit to testify, and the plaintiff is the one who asks them. 'לוא' is read as 'לו,' to him.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
It is written "If he does not (לוא) tell";
phrases.notes: The word for 'not' is spelled with an extra ו, so it can also be read לו, 'to him.'

phrases.aramaic: אִם לוֹ לֹא יַגִּיד – וְנָשָׂא עֲוֹנוֹ,
phrases.english: if he does not tell him, he will carry his sin,
but if he does not tell someone else, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: ״אִם לוֹא יַגִּיד״ כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The spelling לוא is read as לו, 'to him,' so liability applies only when the witness refuses the plaintiff himself, not a messenger or the defendant.

steps.title: Different wordings that count as an oath
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that the witnesses are liable whether the plaintiff said 'I make you swear', 'I command you', or 'I bind you'.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If the plaintiff says 'I put you under oath', 'I command you', or 'I bind you', the witnesses are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens. It lists phrases the plaintiff can use to put the witnesses under a שבועת העדות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plaintiff does not have to say the word 'oath' itself. 'I command you' and 'I bind you' work the same way. If the witnesses then falsely deny knowing testimony, they are liable just as if he had said 'I make you swear'.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
I put you under oath
I command
I bind you
They are liable

phrases.english: MISHNA:
If he says: 'I put you under oath';
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some leave it out. The meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: 'I command you';
'I bind you'. In all of these, they are liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the גמרא finished explaining the earlier cases of שבועת העדות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'I make you swear', 'I command you', and 'I bind you' all count as an oath, so the witnesses are liable.

steps.title: Heaven and earth do not count, but God's names do
steps.stepSummary: An oath 'by heaven and by earth' leaves the witnesses exempt. An oath by any of God's names or descriptions makes them liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he made them swear 'by heaven and by earth', they are exempt. If he used אלף דלת, יוד הי, שדי, צבאות, 'Gracious and Compassionate', 'Slow to Anger', 'Abounding in Kindness', or any other name for God, they are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now asks what the oath must be sworn by. It sets heaven and earth against the names of God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Heaven and earth are only things God created, so an oath by them does not count. Every name and description of God does count, even when the plaintiff did not use the main name. That includes descriptions of God's traits, such as 'Slow to Anger'.

keyTerms.meaning: They are exempt
The name of God that starts with these letters (אדני)
The four-letter name of God
Almighty, a name of God
Other names and descriptions used for God

steps.confusionAlert: The משנה spells out the names by their letters, like 'אלף דלת', so as not to write God's name in full. It still means swearing by the name itself.

phrases.english: If he made them swear 'by heaven and by earth', they are exempt.
'By alef-dalet'; 'by yod-heh';
phrases.notes: These are the first two letters of two of God's names. The משנה writes them this way to avoid spelling out the names.

phrases.english: 'By the Almighty'; 'by the Lord of Hosts';
'By the Gracious and Compassionate One'; 'by the One Slow to Anger';
'By the One Abounding in Kindness'; or by any of the other names for God:
they are liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 18 covered how the oath is worded. This step covers what the oath is sworn by.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath by heaven and earth leaves the witnesses exempt. An oath by any name or description of God makes them liable.

steps.title: Cursing God with these names: a מחלוקת
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר holds that a person who curses God using any of these names is liable. The חכמים exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who curses using any of these names is liable. This is the view of רבי מאיר. The חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves from oaths to a related subject: cursing God with one of these names. It records a disagreement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי מאיר, these names are enough to make a person liable for cursing God, just as they are enough for an oath. The חכמים disagree and exempt him. The usual explanation is that for cursing they require the special name of God, the שם המפורש.

keyTerms.meaning: One who curses
With any of them, meaning these names
The Sages, the majority view

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix the two subjects. Everyone agrees that these names count for an oath. The מחלוקת is only about cursing.

phrases.english: One who curses using any of them is liable;
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Rabbis exempt him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַמְקַלֵּל בְּכוּלָּן חַיָּיב דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the list of names from step 19 and applies it to the separate law of cursing God.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: cursing God with any of these names makes a person liable. חכמים: he is exempt.

steps.title: Cursing a parent with these names: the same מחלוקת
steps.stepSummary: The same disagreement applies to someone who curses his father or mother using one of these names of God.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who curses his father or mother using any of these names is liable. This is the view of רבי מאיר. The חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה repeats the same מחלוקת, this time for cursing a parent with one of God's names.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being liable for cursing a parent also depends on using God's name. So the same question comes up again: do these other names count? רבי מאיר says they do and the חכמים say they do not, the same split as in step 20.

keyTerms.meaning: His father and his mother

steps.whatToRemember: Every name and description of God counts for a שבועת העדות, but heaven and earth do not. For cursing God or cursing a parent, רבי מאיר says these names make a person liable, and the חכמים exempt him.

phrases.english: One who curses his father or his mother using any of them is liable;
these are the words of Rabbi Meir. And the Rabbis exempt him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same מחלוקת from step 20 to cursing a parent.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: cursing a parent with any of these names makes a person liable. חכמים: he is exempt.

steps.title: Cursing yourself or another person with God's name
steps.stepSummary: Anyone who curses himself or his fellow with any of God's names breaks a לא תעשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person curses himself or someone else using any of these names of God, he breaks a negative commandment.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds one more cursing rule: cursing yourself or another Jew with God's name is forbidden by a לא תעשה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 20-21 dealt with cursing God and cursing parents. Here the משנה widens the rule to ordinary people, including the person himself. It only says he 'transgresses a prohibition'; it does not repeat the argument from before.

keyTerms.meaning: one who curses
himself
his fellow, another person
a negative commandment (a 'do not' מצוה)

phrases.english: One who curses himself or his fellow
with any of them transgresses a negative commandment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the cursing laws from God and parents to oneself and others.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cursing oneself or another person with a name of God violates a לא תעשה.

steps.title: 'God shall strike you' is the Torah's own curse
steps.stepSummary: The phrases 'יככה ה׳ אלהים' and 'יככה אלהים' are the curse written in the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says 'The Lord God shall strike you,' or 'God shall strike you,' that is the curse written in the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה returns to the witnesses and gives a clear example of a curse that surely counts: 'God shall strike you' if you don't testify.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the משנה listed oath-words like 'I make you swear.' Now it says that a curse in the form 'God shall strike you' is the standard Torah curse. So witnesses bound this way are surely liable if they deny knowing the testimony.

keyTerms.meaning: may He strike you
a curse (also used for an oath)
written in the Torah

phrases.english: "The Lord God shall strike you,"
and likewise "God shall strike you" –
that is the curse that is written in the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the side topic of cursing to the witnesses' oath, naming the clearest form of curse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'God shall strike you' is the Torah's curse, and it surely makes the witnesses liable.

steps.title: Blessing-style phrases: רבי מאיר versus the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: For 'May He not strike you,' 'May He bless you,' or 'May He do good to you,' רבי מאיר holds the witnesses liable and the חכמים exempt them.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said 'May God not strike you,' 'May God bless you,' or 'May God do good to you' if you testify, רבי מאיר holds them liable and the חכמים say they are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings an argument about phrases that sound like blessings but hint at a curse if the witnesses refuse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר reads the hidden flip side: 'God will bless you if you testify' means 'God won't bless you if you don't.' So it counts as a curse. The חכמים say a curse must be stated outright, so an implied one does not bind the witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: may He bless you
may He do good to you
holds liable
exempt

steps.confusionAlert: These words sound like blessings, but the argument is about whether they work as a curse on witnesses who refuse to testify.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה ends here: the clear curse is 'God shall strike you.' Blessing-style phrases are argued over: רבי מאיר says liable, the חכמים say exempt.

phrases.english: "May He not strike you," or "May He bless you,"
or "May He do good to you" –
Rabbi Meir holds him liable, and the Sages exempt him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the clear curse to unclear, implied curses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An implied curse inside a blessing: רבי מאיר says liable, the חכמים say exempt.

steps.title: What does a plain 'I make you swear' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how 'משביעני עליכם' works when no name of God is said.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said 'I make you swear.' What is he really saying?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and goes back to the משנה's words from Step 18. It asks what 'I make you swear' means, since the plaintiff never mentioned God's name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 taught that an oath needs God's name to count. 'משביעני עליכם' by itself has no name. So the גמרא wants to know how these words can make the witnesses liable.

keyTerms.meaning: the Talmud's discussion of the משנה
I make (you) swear
what is he saying?

phrases.english: GEMARA
"I make you swear" –
what is he saying?
phrases.notes: He never said what he is swearing them by, and no name of God was mentioned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא by questioning the משנה's oath phrases in Step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can 'I make you swear' bind the witnesses without a name of God?

steps.title: רב יהודה: he means the oath written in the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains that each phrase points to the oath, command, or bond 'mentioned in the Torah.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: he means 'I make you swear with the oath mentioned in the Torah,' 'I command you with the command mentioned in the Torah,' 'I bind you with the bond mentioned in the Torah.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers that each of the משנה's short phrases quietly refers to the oath or command written in the Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By pointing to the Torah's oath, the plaintiff brings in God's name, since those Torah oaths are made with God's name. So the words are not empty after all.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what he is saying
a command
a binding obligation, a bond
mentioned in the Torah

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: This is what he is saying:
"I make you swear
with the oath mentioned in the Torah";
"I command you
with the command mentioned in the Torah";
"I bind you
with the bond mentioned in the Torah."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrases refer to the oath, command, or bond mentioned in the Torah, and those include God's name.

steps.title: אביי: 'chaining' is not in the Torah
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רב יהודה from רבי חייא's ברייתא, which counts 'I chain you' even though 'chaining' is not written in the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: But רבי חייא teaches that 'I chain you' also makes them liable. Is 'chaining' written in the Torah?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רב יהודה's explanation. He uses a teaching of רבי חייא that includes a word not found in the Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the phrases only work because they point to a Torah oath, then 'I chain you' should not work, since the Torah never speaks of 'chaining.' Yet רבי חייא says it does work. So the Torah-reference explanation seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: I chain you
is it written?

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
But that which Rabbi Ḥiyya teaches:
"I chain you" – these are liable;
is "chaining" written in the Torah?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי, אֶלָּא הָא דְתָנֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יהודה's answer in Step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's claim that the oath phrases work by pointing to the Torah's wording.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי חייא counts 'I chain you,' a word the Torah never uses, so the phrases cannot depend on matching Torah wording.

steps.title: אביי: The speaker adds the word 'with an oath'
steps.stepSummary: After rejecting רב יהודה's answer, אביי explains that the משנה's phrases work because the speaker adds the word 'בשבועה' to each one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי said the משנה means the person said: 'I make you swear with an oath,' 'I command you with an oath,' 'I bind you with an oath,' 'I chain you with an oath.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a new answer to the question of how 'משביעני עליכם' can work without God's name. He says the speaker added the actual word 'שבועה' (oath).
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה said each phrase points to an oath 'written in the Torah,' but אביי showed that 'chaining' is not in the Torah. So אביי drops that idea. The phrases work because the speaker says the word 'oath' itself, and that holds for 'chaining' too.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; drops the earlier answer and gives a new one
This is what it means
With an oath
I chain you; I bind you as if with chains

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, the phrases in the משנה make the witnesses liable because the speaker says the word 'בשבועה,' not because they point to something written in the Torah.

phrases.english: Rather, Abaye said:
This is what [the mishna] means:
"I make you swear with an oath";
"I command you with an oath";
"I bind you with an oath";
"I chain you with an oath."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב יהודה's answer, which step 27 knocked down.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the wording of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrases work because they point to oaths mentioned in the Torah, as רב יהודה said.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrases work because the speaker actually adds the word 'בשבועה.'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה's phrases mean 'with an oath' (בשבועה). The speaker says the word oath, which also covers 'כובלכם', so nothing depends on the wording appearing in the Torah.

steps.title: The משנה's list of God's names and descriptions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, which lists the names and descriptions of God that make the witnesses liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: if he made them swear by אלף דלת, by יוד הי, by שדי, by צבאות, by Gracious and Compassionate, by Slow to Anger, or by Abounding in Kindness, the witnesses are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next words of the משנה, which list names of God and descriptions of God used in the oath. This sets up the question coming next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה mixes real names, like the four-letter name and שדי, with descriptions, like חנון ורחום. It treats them all the same: an oath with any of them makes the witnesses liable.

keyTerms.meaning: The name of God that begins with the letters א-ד, spelled out by letter out of respect
The four-letter name of God, which begins with the letters י-ה
The Almighty, a name of God
Lord of Hosts, a name of God
Gracious and Compassionate, words that describe God

phrases.english: "By alef-dalet"; "by yod-heh";
phrases.notes: These are God's holy names. The text only says their first two letters so it doesn't write the full name.

phrases.english: "By Shaddai"; "by Tzevaot";
"By Gracious and Compassionate";
"By Slow to Anger"; "by Abounding in Kindness."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath given to witnesses with any of these names or descriptions of God makes them liable.

steps.title: Are Gracious and Compassionate really names of God?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the משנה means that חנון ורחום are real names of God, and gets ready to show a source that disagrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that 'Gracious and Compassionate' are names of God? But compare this to a ברייתא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is surprised that the משנה treats חנון ורחום like real names of God. It announces that it will bring a ברייתא that seems to say otherwise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה makes witnesses liable for an oath 'by Gracious and Compassionate,' it seems to treat these words as holy names. The word 'ורמינהי' tells us a contradicting source is coming next.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? Used to question what something implies
Names, here meaning holy names of God
Compare it to this source, which seems to contradict it

phrases.english: Is that to say that "Gracious and Compassionate"
are names [of God]?!
But contrast this with [a baraita]:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions what the משנה in step 29 implies.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's listing of חנון ורחום as words that make an oath binding.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only a real name of God should give an oath its force, and another source treats חנון ורחום as mere descriptions.

steps.title: The ברייתא: names of God that may not be erased
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says some names of God may be erased and some may not. It lists the ones that may not be erased, like אל, אלהים, the four-letter name, שדי and צבאות.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are names of God that may be erased and names that may not be erased. These may not be erased: אל, אלהיך, אלהים, אלהיכם, אהיה אשר אהיה, אלף דלת, יוד הי, שדי, צבאות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the first half of the ברייתא, which lists the holy names of God that may never be erased. Note that חנון ורחום are not on this list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא sorts words about God into two groups. This first group holds the true holy names, which are too holy to erase. חנון ורחום are left out of it, which hints they are not true names.

keyTerms.meaning: May be erased
May not be erased, because they are holy
I Will Be What I Will Be, a name of God
For example

phrases.english: There are names that may be erased,
and there are names that may not be erased.
These are the names that may not be erased:
For example, "Kel," "Your God,"
"Elokim," "Your God" (plural),
"I Will Be What I Will Be,"
"alef-dalet" and "yod-heh,"
"Shaddai," "Tzevaot" —
these may not be erased.

steps.triggerLanguage: יֵשׁ שֵׁמוֹת שֶׁנִּמְחָקִין, וְיֵשׁ שֵׁמוֹת שֶׁאֵין נִמְחָקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the source announced by 'ורמינהי' in step 30.
steps.raayaObject: That only certain words count as true holy names of God.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about which names of God may be erased.

steps.title: The ברייתא: descriptions of God that may be erased, including Gracious and Compassionate
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the ברייתא lists descriptions of God that may be erased, and חנון ורחום are among them. That is the contradiction with the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But 'the Great,' 'the Mighty,' 'the Awesome,' 'the Glorious,' 'the Powerful,' 'the Courageous,' 'the Strong,' 'Gracious and Compassionate,' 'Slow to Anger,' and 'Abounding in Kindness' may be erased.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now lists words that describe God and may be erased. חנון ורחום, ארך אפים and רב חסד are on this list, so they seem to be only descriptions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If חנון ורחום may be erased, they are not holy names. So how can our משנה say an oath 'by Gracious and Compassionate' makes the witnesses liable? The גמרא has set up the contradiction and will need to answer it.

keyTerms.meaning: The Great, the Mighty, and the Awesome; words that praise God
Slow to anger
Abounding in kindness
But; marks the second group

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does not say these words have no holiness at all. It only says they are descriptions of God, not His actual names, so the strict ban on erasing does not apply to them.
steps.whyThisMatters: The ברייתא sets out a real halacha about which written words for God may be erased. Now the גמרא must explain how the משנה can treat these descriptions as strong enough for an oath.

phrases.english: But "the Great," "the Mighty," "the Awesome,"
"the Glorious," "the Powerful," "the Courageous,"
"the Strong," "Gracious and Compassionate,"
"Slow to Anger" and "Abounding in Kindness" —
these may be erased.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא, and its second half makes the contradiction with the משנה clear.
steps.raayaObject: That חנון ורחום are descriptions of God, not true names.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's list of words for God that may be erased.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that an oath 'בחנון ורחום', 'בארך אפים' or 'ברב חסד' makes the witnesses liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lists חנון ורחום, ארך אפים and רב חסד among words that may be erased. That makes them descriptions, not holy names, so an oath by them should not bind the witnesses.

steps.title: אביי: The משנה Means 'By the One Who Is Gracious'
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers the contradiction. The משנה is talking about someone who swears 'בְּמִי שֶׁהוּא חַנּוּן', meaning 'by the One Who is gracious', not about the plain word חנון.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Our משנה means 'by the One Who is gracious.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא. He says the משנה is talking about the phrase 'by the One Who is gracious.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא was talking about the plain word חנון, which is only a description and may be erased. The משנה is talking about someone who swears 'by Him Who is gracious', and that wording points directly at God Himself. So it counts for an oath, and the two sources no longer contradict.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
'By the One Who is gracious', a phrase that points at God Himself

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not saying that חנון is a holy name that may not be erased. The ברייתא still stands: the plain word may be erased. Only the full phrase 'by the One Who is gracious' works for an oath.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer shows that an oath can be binding even with a description of God, as long as the wording clearly refers to God Himself.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Our משנה means 'by the One Who is gracious'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in steps 30–32 between the משנה and the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the wording of the משנה (the cases are different)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the משנה treats the bare words חנון ורחום as real names of God, which goes against the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה means a person who swears 'by the One Who is gracious'. That phrase refers to God Himself, while the bare word stays an erasable description.
